comparison.objective: Candidate sets a DRG 80 gripper’s opening-stop screw to 90°, locks the setting, removes the tools, and verifies retained opening through repeated actuation. PR-216 instead captures an external reference angle with a bevel gauge, carries it to a board, and transfers it by drawing a guided line.
comparison.physical_skill: Candidate tests coaxial driver and thin-wrench seating, coupled screw/jam-nut adjustment, and bimanual countertorque that prevents locknut tightening from disturbing the stop. PR-216 explicitly has no locking screw: it fits a passive-friction hinged blade to two faces, releases the blade gripper, transports the gauge without changing its angle, seats it, and guides a marker.
comparison.success_condition: Candidate rewards target opening accuracy, seated/retained nuts, hands-off repeat-cycle return, limited stop drift, tool withdrawal, and clearance, with loss revocation. PR-216 rewards fixture fit, visible release and retained angle during carry, board seating, then line coverage, tick proximity, straightness, gap/width limits, absence of stray marks, and nib clearance. All seven available spec versions provide numeric rubric details; none are materially missing for this comparison.
comparison.reason: Both involve adjusting and retaining an angle, but PR-216 relies on passive hinge friction to transfer a measured angle into a drawn mark, whereas the candidate tests active preservation of a screw setting against jam-nut reaction followed by functional cycling; these are meaningfully different mechanisms, manipulation abilities, and outcomes.

review_notes: Bevel gauge angle capture/transfer. Compare measurement/locking, all original versions; verify friction hinge versus lockscrew claim.
